claims.text: Superconducting behavior in high-entropy superconducting alloys is primarily governed by electron–phonon coupling strength.
Intrinsic chemical disorder produces local lattice distortions that modulate electron–phonon coupling.
The proposed as-deposited nanocrystalline alloy has a high degree of chemical disorder and associated lattice distortions.
Controlled thermal annealing can partially relax lattice distortions while retaining the alloy's overall composition.
Local lattice distortions and grain-boundary disorder affect the density of states at the Fermi level.
Local lattice distortions and grain-boundary disorder affect electron–phonon interactions.
Thermal annealing will reduce the extreme local lattice distortions in the as-deposited state.
Relaxation of local lattice distortions will modify electron–phonon coupling.
If lattice distortions enhance electron–phonon interactions, reducing those distortions may lower the superconducting transition temperature.
If excessive disorder suppresses coherent pairing, modestly reducing distortion may enhance superconductivity.
Changes in local structure mediate changes in the electronic pairing interactions underlying superconductivity.
Annealing will cause a measurable shift in superconducting transition temperature, although its direction is not specified.
Annealing will modify the alloy's critical magnetic field.
The magnitude of the superconducting-property change will correlate with the extent of measured lattice-distortion relaxation.
The proposed mechanism applies when superconductivity is not overwhelmed by magnetic impurities or a fully amorphous structure.
The mechanism may have negligible impact when the microstructure is already optimized or further disorder modification does not appreciably change electron–phonon coupling.
Disorder can beneficially enhance local electron–phonon interactions.
Direct evidence linking lattice-distortion relaxation to superconducting performance in these systems is currently limited.

contradictions.description: The mechanism and prediction allow Tc to move either upward or downward, yet a change in the 'opposite direction' is listed as falsifying. No predicted direction is defined, so an opposite-direction result cannot be identified.
